name: K-Guard to Matrix
description: Transition from K-guard into the matrix (under-hip reversal) to create a backside angle for back takes, reverse leg drags, or leg entanglement finishes.
shortInstruction: K-guard to matrix: rotate your hips over, hook the far hip, and come up on the backside.
summary: The K-guard to matrix transition is the most powerful back-side entry in modern no-gi. When you are in K-guard and they defend the leg entanglement by stepping back or posting, you rotate your hips over your own shoulder and 'matrix' under their hips — reversing your angle from under them to behind them. From the matrix, you can take the back, enter a reverse leg drag, or finish a heel hook from the backside.
whyItWorks: The matrix reverses the inside/outside relationship — you go from being underneath to being behind them.
It turns their defense (stepping back) into your offense (back take).
The matrix does not require strength — it is a hip rotation and angle change.
Danaher principle: the matrix solves the problem of the opponent stepping out of K-guard.
commonMistakes: Trying to matrix without controlling their far arm — they will spin and face you.
Rotating over your head instead of your shoulder — this can injure your neck.
Stopping at the matrix instead of flowing to the finish — matrix is transitional, not final.
Losing the leg entanglement during the matrix transition.
coachingCues: Rotate over the shoulder, not the head.
Control the arm, hook the hip, go behind.
If they step back, matrix forward.
Matrix is the tunnel — back take is the destination.
safetySummary: Do not rotate over the top of your head — always rotate over your shoulder to protect your neck and spine.
When entering the matrix, keep your legs active to prevent knee strain.
If you feel pressure on your lower back during the rotation, bail out and reset.
keyCorrections: If they don't go with the matrix, you lost momentum — maintain speed through the rotation.
If you can't take the back, your angle is wrong — walk your hips closer to theirs before rotating.
If they flatten you in the matrix, you didn't commit fully — go harder or bail out.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: K-guard established: opponent steps back or posts → rotate hips over shoulder → hook far hip → take back or enter reverse leg drag.

decisionTree.action: The matrix works because the K-guard already has you under their center — the rotation just reverses the angle.
attack the leg entanglement from K-guard instead.

moneyDetails: Rotate over your shoulder, not your head — place your head to the side as you roll.
Hook their far hip with your top leg as you rotate — this prevents them from following you.
Control their near arm throughout the rotation to prevent them from peeling you off.
When you land in the matrix, immediately look for the back take — don't pause.
nextStep: After the matrix, learn the back take from K-guard and the reverse leg drag entry.
fixItFast: Matrix feels clunky? Practice the hip rotation on the ground without a partner — shoulder-over, not head-over.
Can't take the back? You didn't hook the far hip — re-establish the hip hook before coming up.
They follow you through the matrix? Your arm control is weak — grip their triceps or sleeve tighter.
